class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Dancing Queen: An ABBA Salute performs at Andersonville’s Midsommarfest on June 13, 2026. From left, singer and guitarist Justin Horvath-Adair, backing vocalist Elya Bottiger, lead singer Amanda Horvath-Adair, drummer Keith Daproza, lead singer Cheryl Jennison Daproza, bass player Davide Pezzini, and pianist Micky York.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Steve Jurkovic/Provided by Amanda Horvath-Adair.</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Dancing Queen: An ABBA Salute started in 2004. Tribute bands typically cover one band or artist. Dancing Queen used to be called ABBA Salute, but the original Swedish quartet has a strong legal team which prohibits tribute bands from using “ABBA” in the main portion of its name. Dancing Queen is something close to local celebrities, and some shows book more than a year in advance.</p><p><b>Members:</b> Micky York as Benny Andersson on vocals, keyboard and accordion; Amanda Horvath-Adair as Agnetha Fältskog on vocals; Justin Horvath-Adair as Björn Ulvaeus on vocals; Cheryl Jennison Daproza as Anni-Frid Lyngstad on vocals; Davide Pezzini on bass; Keith Daproza on drums</p><p>Behind the scenes, members of Dancing Queen double as the band’s social media marketer, website administrator, costume designer and business manager. While the band could make this their only gig, they all have day jobs, mostly at local colleges. When Micky York isn’t wearing a pair of flashy bell-bottoms, you might find him teaching at Columbia College and the College of DuPage. The married Horvath-Adairs work at Roosevelt University, while Cheryl Jennison Daproza is in communications at Shure Incorporated.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.dancingqueenband.com/schedule" target="_blank" ><b><u>Where to see them</u></b></a>: All over the Chicago area, all summer long. “We’re unavoidable. We’re not sorry about it,” Amanda Horvath-Adair said.</p><p><b>Artists/songs they cover:</b> All things ABBA</p><p><b>Why they do it:</b> Justin Horvath-Adair compared it to acting in his favorite theater production. When you’re in a play, he said, you build close relationships that are hard to maintain when the production ends. But with Dancing Queen, “there’s no time limit, and they become a second family.”</p><p>Amanda Horvath-Adair said it’s a privilege to perform in front of so many people: “How did I get so lucky to do this, and then to like the people I do it with? entries.title: Bears Training Camp Report: Practice No. 1
entries.summary: <p>Breaking down the Bears' Wednesday training camp practice, the first of the year:</p><h3>What happened</h3><p>As he does on the first day of every training camp, defensive coordinator Dennis Allen put his healthy players through 40 up-downs Wednesday. Safety Coby Bryant joked he planned on telling Allen they were too easy.</p><p>"It's a mindset thing," Bryant said. "We’re going to deal with way harder stuff than 40 up-downs.”</p><p>The practice was, by Collective Bargaining Agreement mandate, light — about one hour and 15 minutes on the backfields of Halas Hall. The team won’t wear pads until Monday.</p><p>The highlight of practice came when, during a long special teams period, second-year receiver Luther Burden caught a punt with his left arm — and then, without dropping the first ball, caught the next one with his right. </p><p>Later in the period, punter Tory Taylor booted a knuckleball that landed inside the 5-yard line and bounced perfectly sideways, drawing a few gasps.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">The highlight of the <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/Bears?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#Bears</a>’ first practice: Luther Burden catching a punt with each arm. No photos allowed during that period so … <a href="https://t.co/35fTz9MXU6">pic.twitter.com/35fTz9MXU6</a></p>— Patrick Finley (@patrickfinley) <a href="https://x.com/patrickfinley/status/2082485903646130265?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 29, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3>Position Battle Watch</h3><h3></h3><p>With Kyler Gordon <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/07/28/bears-training-camp-kyler-gordon-get-healthy-ben-johnson-ryan-poles-calf-injury-cornerback" target="_blank" >out with a calf injury</a>, cornerback Jaylon Jones and cornerback/safety Cam Lewis took snaps in the slot. As was the case in the spring, Braxton Jones functioned as the first-team left tackle.</p><h3>What’s next</h3><h3></h3><p>The Bears will practice at 8:30 a.m. Thursday. As was the case Wednesday, there will be no fans in attendance.</p>

entries.title: Boy, 15, shot in Englewood
entries.summary: <p>A 15-year-old boy was shot Tuesday night in Englewood on the South Side, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The teen was found with a gunshot wound to the back in the 7000 block of South Hermitage Avenue around 11:30 p.m., police said in a statement.</p><p>He was taken in good condition to Comer Children's Hospital, police said. No arrests were reported.</p>

entries.title: 3 injured, including teen boy, in ATV crash in Belmont Cragin
entries.summary: <p>Three people were injured after an SUV and an all-terrain vehicle crashed in Belmont Cragin on Tuesday night. </p><p>A woman was turning left into a parking lot in the 4800 block of West Diversey Avenue when she collided with an ATV driven by a 22-year-old man and a 16-year-old passenger just after 9 p.m., Chicago police said. </p><p>The man was in critical condition and the teenage boy in good condition, police said. They were taken to Lutheran General Hospital.</p><p>The woman was in good condition and was taken to Illinois Masonic Medical Center, police said. </p><p>Citation were pending, police said. </p>

entries.title: Bears didn't add a relevant edge rusher — and don't plan to now
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> began the offseason saying they needed to rush the passer better.</p><p>Then they didn’t sign an edge rusher of significance. Or trade for one. Or draft one. Or even grab a veteran on the eve of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/07/27/bears-ben-johnson-ryan-poles-training-camp-four-questions-caleb-williams-braxton-jones-kyler-gordon-dayo-odeyingbo-nfl" target="_blank" >training camp</a>.</p><p>When the Bears took the field for the first day of camp Wednesday, they had the same top three edge rushers that helped produce the second-worst defensive line pass-rush win rate in the NFL last year.</p><p>It doesn’t sound like that’s going to change any time soon.</p><p>“We’ve got to make sure we know our team,” general manager Ryan Poles said Tuesday. “So, we evaluate on a daily basis and see what we need to do.”</p><p>If the Bears decide they need to add one of the few veterans left on the free-agent market — Joey Bosa, Jadeveon Clowney and Brandon Graham are among them — it will be only after they’ve exhausted every option on their roster.</p><p>“We can cross that bridge if we ever need to go across it,” Poles said.</p><p>The fact is, if the Bears thought there was a fit on the free agent market, they would have signed one by now. The household names who are available are aging role players. The one star that might prove available, Maxx Crosby, might just stay with the Raiders. When the team made him available before a scuttled trade to the Ravens, the Bears thought the Raiders' asking price on him was too prohibitive, anyway.</p><p>Any long-term answers at edge rusher will have to wait until next offseason. Until then, will rely once again on Montez Sweat, Austin Booker and Dayo Odeyingbo. Sweat will miss the first few practices because of an illness, while Odeyingbo's return to health has been a pleasant surprise after he tore his Achilles' tendon following eight games — and just one sack.</p><p>Minutes before the Bears took the field Wednesday morning, defensive coordinator Dennis Allen was as animated as he’s been in his tenure with the team when describing how the team needed to improve on passing downs.</p><p>"There's a lot been made of the pass rush, right?" Allen said. "There's no example of team defense that it's better exemplified than in pass defense. Because I don't care how good your pass rush is, if [defensive backs] don't cause the quarterback to have to reset or get to his second or third read you're not getting to him. And I don't care how good your coverage is, if you can't get to the quarterback and disrupt him they're going to throw completions. So, I think we've got to get better at pass defense, all right? And I think that's both elements working together. And so I think that's what our focus is. </p><p>"Our focus is not necessarily this area and this area, it's completely as a team, how are we going to improve as a team. And I think we all take a part of that. Coaches, players, scheme, fundamentals and technique, all of those things play a part in that."<br></p>

entries.title: Man stabbed in Hegewisch
entries.summary: <p>A man was hospitalized in serious condition after being stabbed Tuesday evening in Hegewisch on the Far South Side, Chicago police said.</p><p>The man, 37, was standing outside at 8:15 p.m. in the 13000 block of South Houston Avenue when an another man approached and attacked him with a sharp object, police said in a statement.</p><p>He suffered a laceration to his arm and was taken to Trinity Hospital in serious condition, according to police, who reported no arrests.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Man killed, another wounded in South Shore shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man was killed and another wounded in a shooting late Tuesday in the South Shore neighborhood, Chicago police said.</p><p>The shooting happened around 11:55 p.m. in the 6700 block of South Chappel Avenue, police said in a statement.</p><p>One man, 35, suffered gunshot wounds to the back and chest and was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where police said he was later pronounced, police said.</p><p>The other man, 42, was shot in his back and arm, and was taken to the same hospital in critical condition, police said.</p><p>Police said no one was in custody.</p>

entries.title: 3 injured in crash involving 2 motorcycles on I-290
entries.summary: <p>Three people were injured in a crash involving two motorcycles and a passenger vehicle Tuesday night on Interstate 290 near suburban Hillside.</p><p>Deputies responded to the crash in the eastbound lanes near Wolf Road around 8:50 p.m., according a statement from Illinois State Police.</p><p>Three people were taken to area hospitals with injuries, police said. The roadway was temporarily shut down. No further information was released.</p>

entries.title: Man dies after being found with gunshot wound in West Pullman
entries.summary: <p>A 43-year-old man was pronounced dead after he was found outside with a gunshot wound to the chest early Wednesday in West Pullman, police said.</p><p>The incident occurred about 12:15 a.m. in the 11600 block of South Halsted Street, Chicago police said in a statement.</p><p>He was taken in critical condition to Christ Hospital, where he was later pronounced. Police reported no arrests.</p>

Park, Libertyville and portions of the South Side. He also says he has encountered them, and tried to capture one 1976 experience in his painting titled "In the Daytime, Bobba!" which depicts a white spaceship hovering over Earth against an intense blue sky. </p><p>The painting is displayed with other works in his new art show, "Mothership," now showing at Mariane Ibrahim Gallery in West Town through Sept. 5.</p><p>"He is a pre-internet architect of Afrofuturism vocabulary and imagery," said Mariane Ibrahim, a French-Somali gallerist who also owns spaces in Paris and Mexico City.</p><p>"To think about Black bodies in the cosmic [realm], as technological bodies, he was one of the first artists to engage with that," Ibrahim said. "My parents used to look at him like, 'He’s totally crazy.' But this craziness had the color of my skin, so I felt entitled to be crazy as well, to free myself."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wudhdlk-l-dl/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p>What's the most memorable Lollapalooza performance you've seen? Maybe the sounds of the lake and the waves hitting the rocks. Perhaps the birds chirping at sunrise." — <i>Brice Notardonato Ellett</i></p><p>"The water lapping against the barriers on Lake Michigan." — <i>Daniel Christie</i></p><p>"The crack of a cold one." — <i>Bryan Murillo</i></p><p>"My daughter's voice, birds in the morning, rain hitting my window late at night, cars driving by." — <i>Mimi Gates</i></p><p>"Cicadas." — <i>Dennis Willis</i></p><p>"I'd miss the voices of my loved ones, and the laughter that ensues when we're together." — <i>Christine Bock</i></p><p>"Live music, casual conversation, my feet on a sidewalk as I walk wherever I want to go." — <i>Paul Lockwood</i></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Eydie Cubarrubia</p><hr><p><i>The Chicago Sun-Times is a nonprofit supported by readers like you. entries.title: How Blackhawks rookie Roman Kantserov is preparing for the NHL: 'I can do this'
entries.summary: <p>As a kid, Roman Kantserov remembers watching Transformers and Spider-Man movies with Russian subtitles.</p><p>As he prepares for his first season with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>, the 21-year-old forward from Magnitogorsk, Russia, is now watching those same movies in English.</p><p>That's one part of Kantserov's admirable effort to fast-track his English fluency, which should not only make his adjustment to life in Chicago easier but also help him communicate on the ice with his new teammates.</p><p>He was inspired by the import players on his KHL team, which coincidentally included two former Rockford IceHogs: Luke Johnson and Robin Press.</p><p>"Talking with the boys, they say, 'Roma, learn English. It helps you,'" Kantserov said Wednesday. "I think right now, [my] English is not bad, but I need to learn [more].'"</p><p>During <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/05/08/blackhawks-sign-roman-kantserov-nhl-contract-russia-prospects" target="_blank" >entry-level contract</a> negotiations in May, Hawks general manager Kyle Davidson was "extremely impressed" by Kantserov's ability to talk without a translator, which assured him Kantserov wouldn't need any "special accommodations" from a language perspective this season.</p><p>And Kantserov's English has only improved further since then, because he has been living in the United States — training with a group of Russians and Rangers in Stamford, Connecticut — since late June.</p><p>"In one month, walking around New York and around Stamford, [when I] go to buy coffee or go to shop, of course I listen to how everyone is saying [things] in English," he said. "I learn it."</p><p>Kantserov hopped over to Chicago for a couple days this week for the NHL Players Association's rookie showcase, which Hawks prospect Sacha Boisvert also attended. </p><p>The brief stop in Chicago gave him an opportunity to tour Hawks facilities and meet some staff, including skills coach Kendall Coyne Schofield and strength coach Juan Gonzalez.</p><p>Expectations are lofty for Kantserov after he led the KHL in goals last season, burying 36 in 63 games. Davidson hasn't been shy about penciling him into a first-line winger spot next to Connor Bedard, and Bedard being sidelined for the first month of the season won't change that.</p><p>"Right now, Connor has the injury. It's sad news," Kantserov said. "But Chicago signed Patrick Kane. The legend has come back. It's awesome. </p><p>"He's the greatest American player, all-time scorer, and this is a very good opportunity to play with him. Of course, if we play together with Bedard, maybe we can find the chemistry."</p><p>Kantserov hasn't yet talked to Kane, but he said he did text Bedard: "Faster recovery. We need you."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Spencer Knight welcoming Roman Kantserov Stateside! <br><br>(IG: slknight35) <a href="https://t.co/PehX7zfRqr">pic.twitter.com/PehX7zfRqr</a></p>— CHGO Blackhawks (@CHGO_Blackhawks) <a href="https://x.com/CHGO_Blackhawks/status/2072106110769856738?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">June 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>He has spent the most time so far with Hawks goalie Spencer Knight, a Connecticut native. They haven't been on the same training schedule aside from one camp, but they have had dinners together.</p><p>"[Spencer is] a good guy," Kantserov said. "He helps me with talking. He says, 'Chicago is a great city, great fans, great organization.' And I see this right now. It's absolutely awesome. I'm excited, waiting for the season."</p><p>Kantserov currently has the sixth-highest odds for the Calder Trophy, per FanDuel, while Hawks rookie forward Anton Frondell is tied for fourth. Flyers forward Porter Martone, Maple Leafs forward Gavin McKenna and Sharks forward Ivar Stenberg are the three favorites.</p><p>But there's no guarantee everything clicks right away for Kantserov. He has a strong, sturdy build, but at 5-9, he's undeniably short by NHL standards.</p><p>And even though the KHL is still arguably the second-best league in the world, it has weakened over the past decade, so the NHL represents a large step up in competition.</p><p>"I need to improve my skills, improve my thinking," Kantserov said. "I need to think smarter and faster, because here is [an] absolutely different level. It should be hard, but it's not impossible. I think I can do this."</p>

entries.title: New Illinois law lets courts wade into pet disputes involving non-married couples
entries.summary: <p>People who share a pet will be able to go to court to fight for custody of their furry companion under a state law newly enacted by Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker.</p><p>The measure creates a legal framework for unmarried people, like separated couples or roommates, to fight to keep their dog, cat or horse when they no longer live with the person they shared it with.</p><p>The new law permits courts to consider several factors when deciding who gets custody of a pet between two unmarried people.</p><p>Those factors include the physical and emotional well-being of the animal, who financially supports it, and the environment the pet would live in.</p><p>Divorcing couples were already able to fight for custody of a shared pet in Illinois.</p><p>State Rep. Barbara Hernandez (D-Aurora), who sponsored the legislation, said people reached out to her after losing custody of their pet because they weren’t married to the other owner.</p><p>“Either they were in an abusive relationship, and the partner used their pet as leverage to stay in the relationship, or there were military people that had an emotional support animal and unfortunately had to leave them behind because their partner wanted to keep it,” she said. “There was no path for them to fight for the animal.”</p><p>Hernandez said the new law will allow more people to protect their loved pets, and people should prepare if they’re in a situation where they may have to go to court for their pet.</p><p>“Make sure you have all the proof of the vet bills, the food bills, and everything to make sure that you can establish yourself as a primary owner of your pet,” she said.</p><p>Jane McBride, CEO of Illinois Humane, a Springfield-based non-profit animal shelter, worked with Hernandez on the bill and said pet custody battles aren’t a new phenomenon.</p><p>She said in cases of divorce, the court must consider the emotional and physical well-being of the animal whereas in cases of unmarried pet owners, it had not been an issue that a court could consider.</p><p>“Animals are property, but they're protected property throughout many avenues of the law in Illinois,” she said. “So this amendment provides guidance to the courts should this be an issue.”</p><p>McBride also said these cases can involve roommates who disproportionately care for the animal. They then have to prove to the court that they are the main caretaker.</p><p>“You either have to be the owner and have that kind of documentation, or you have to have some kind of basis to show that you're entitled to possession of the animal,” she said.</p><p>The new law goes into effect Jan. 1.</p>

entries.title: Residente de Lake View demanda al gobierno federal por allanar su casa y detener a trabajador durante operativo
entries.summary: <p>Un hombre de Lake View demandó al gobierno federal el martes alegando que agentes de inmigración entraron en su casa sin una orden judicial y arrestaron a un trabajador de la construcción que había contratado en pleno apogeo de la campaña de deportaciones de la administración de Trump el otoño pasado.</p><p>Leo Feler viajaba por trabajo la mañana del 24 de octubre cuando encendió su cámara Ring y vio a agentes federales enmascarados descendiendo sobre su domicilio en la cuadra 3300 al norte de Lakewood Avenue, según la demanda federal. Iban persiguiendo a un grupo de trabajadores que Feler contrató para reparar ventanas.</p><p>Usando el micrófono de la cámara, Feler les dijo a los agentes que estaban invadiendo su propiedad y les exigió que se retiraran de su terreno, según la demanda. Un inquilino, que estaba en la casa en ese momento, también exigió ver una orden, pero fue ignorado.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8a0000" name="module-8a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Un trabajador fue arrestado por agentes federales y docenas de vecinos de Feler fueron rociados con gas lacrimógeno mientras protestaban. Feler regresó a su casa y encontró varios "charcos de sangre" y docenas de miles de dólares en daños a su propiedad, según la demanda.</p><p>Está exigiendo una indemnización por daños y perjuicios al gobierno federal y a todos los agentes individuales involucrados.</p><p>"No había razón alguna para que esta redada se realizara en mi propiedad", comentó Feler en una conferencia de prensa el martes frente a su casa. "No había nada ilegal pasando en mi propiedad. Eran solo trabajadores haciendo construcción", añadió.</p><p>Esa mañana, los agentes de la Oficina de Aduanas y Protección Fronteriza (CBP) ya habían estado en <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/10/24/federales-realizan-arrestos-noroeste-lanzan-lacrimgeno-calle-residencial" target="_blank" >otros vecindarios del norte</a>.</p><p>Luego aceleraron en sentido contrario por la tranquila cuadra de Lake View y vieron a cuatro trabajadores "comiendo tranquilamente" afuera de la casa de Feler, según la demanda. Los agentes salieron de dos camionetas y comenzaron a perseguir a los trabajadores, quienes corrieron detrás de la cerca de 6 pies de Feler y cerraron la puerta.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/dKXPordbAnc?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Feds make arrests, deploy tear gas in Lake View"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Al no poder romper el candado de la puerta, los agentes empezaron a trepar la cerca y persiguieron a los trabajadores por la propiedad de Feler, entrando a su patio trasero, balcón y garaje separado de la casa, dice la demanda. A uno de los cuatro trabajadores lo siguieron hasta el garaje y lo detuvieron.</p><p>Cuando los agentes llevaron al trabajador de vuelta al frente, docenas de vecinos se habían reunido afuera para protestar por el arresto y exigir ver una orden. Mientras los agentes seguían por la calle, lanzaron al menos dos cartuchos de gas lacrimógeno hacia el grupo de vecinos. Los testigos dijeron que no oyeron ninguna advertencia antes de que se desplegara el gas.</p><p>"Al final de la redada, cuando estos agentes federales se estaban retirando, sin que nadie les impidiera retroceder, se les oyó gritar: 'Lancen el gas lacrimógeno solo por diversión'", comentó Feler.</p><p>"Eso da una idea de lo que se trató esta redada", añadió. "Para ellos fue solo diversión, pero para mí fue traumático".</p><p>Después de la redada, el gobierno admitió que no tenía una orden ni motivo alguno para creer que se estaba cometiendo actividad delictiva en o cerca de la propiedad de Feler, según la demanda. Feler comenzó a trabajar con un abogado de inmigración para brindar apoyo al trabajador detenido. Más tarde supo que el trabajador no tenía antecedentes penales y que había estado pagando impuestos. Se ordenó la liberación del trabajador de la custodia federal tres semanas después del arresto.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/x0ItYUijCgk?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Chicago Homeowner Sues After Warrantless CBP Raid | Press Conference"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Feler <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/10/31/lake-view-federal-cpd-immigration-raid" target="_blank" >intentó presentar previamente</a> un informe ante la Policía de Chicago, pero comentó que básicamente lo rechazaron en la estación —dos veces. Una estación le permitió presentar un informe por daños a la propiedad, pero luego le llamaron para informarle que la policía no continuaría con el caso.</p><p>"Así que aquí estoy ahora", agregó Feler. "Y presento este caso por respeto, admiración y deber hacia mi país, hacia nuestra Constitución, hacia mis vecinos, que fueron rociados con gas lacrimógeno mientras trataban de defender mi casa, hacia mis inquilinos, que tuvieron que soportar la redada… hacia mi familia y hacia mí mismo".</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: TF North basketball coach and former Simeon star Tim Bankston found fatally shot in Auburn Gresham home
entries.summary: <p>Tim Bankston, a South Side basketball legend at Simeon and the current boys basketball coach at TF North High School in Lansing, was found fatally shot Wednesday morning inside a home in Auburn Gresham on the South Side, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Bankston, 60, was found unresponsive with a gunshot wound to his abdomen around 10 a.m. in the 7600 block of South Emerald Street, police said in a statement. He was pronounced dead at the scene, police said.</p><p>Police said no one else was injured and reported no arrests. No additional details were released.</p><p>A large crowd of family, former Simeon teammates and former players gathered on South Emerald to mourn Bankston and support each other on Wednesday afternoon. </p><p>"I was coming from an event and saw the tape," Ald. David Moore (17th) said. "The police had not put out the report to me yet. I was on my way back home and my friend told me he was goneI cannot believe this. It just brings back all the things with Benji. It was not supposed to go like this. He was not supposed to go like this."</p><p>Bankston was a Simeon teammate of Ben "Benji" Wilson, who was shot and killed on the South Side in November of 1984, shortly before his senior basketball season was about to begin. Wilson was the top-rated player in the country. </p><p>Bankston went on to lead Simeon to the state title in 1984. He played on one year at Bradley and two years at Loyola. He's been the head coach at TF North since 2002. </p><p>"We don’t know what happened yet," Sean Wright, Bankston's brother, said. "They said they found my brother’s body and to come as fast as you can. From what the officer said it looked like he had been laying there overnight."</p><p><i>Check back for more on this developing story...</i></p>

entries.title: Prominent Chicago dance venue damaged by flood following heavy storms
entries.summary: <p>Ruth Page Center for the Arts may be facing considerable damage to its 100-year-old building following <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/27/weather-storms-heat-wind" >heavy thunderstorms</a> on Monday.</p><p>The Near North Side dance organization, located at 1016 N. Dearborn St., experienced flooding in lower-level areas of its venue, including dance studios, a women’s restroom, costume storage, utility closets and sewing rooms. While waiting on a full assessment of repairs from the insurance company, the nonprofit is accepting <a class="Link" href="https://fundraise.givesmart.com/e/Ddh_Bw?vid=1rkad2&fbclid=PAcGRvZgRleHRuA2FlbQIxMQBzcnRjBmFwcF9pZAwyNTYyODEwNDA1NTgAAaf-xdm4LwTOR52NI5xO1fwbG9NjDTRvqIPgUqYr4X9DDAEl-qa0IoUz6NvPjQ_aem_WWiIGB6KucQQ7K4Oc5-1_Q" target="_blank" ><u>donations on its websites</u></a> to help purchase equipment, including extra wet/dry vacuum cleaners and industrial fans.</p><p>Classes were canceled yesterday, but they have since resumed. However, the organization is working out logistics for its upcoming events, which include a performance by Summer Dance Bootcamp students on Friday and a Fall Open House on Sunday.</p><div Officials at Morton Arboretum were among those that said their grounds remained closed Wednesday for cleanup.</p><p>Leaders at Ruth Page Center say flooding is an ongoing issue, and the setback comes at a time of economic strain for the Chicago arts sector. entries.title: Indicted ex-Loretto Hospital executive no longer fighting extradition to the U.S., attorney says
entries.summary: <p>The former chief financial officer of Loretto Hospital who left the United States before federal grand jurors handed up two fraud indictments against him will no longer contest extradition from Serbia, where he has been held in custody since November, his lawyer told a judge Wednesday.</p><p>That means Anosh Ahmed might soon return to Chicago to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/08/02/loretto-hospital-anosh-ahmed-sameer-suhail-medicare-fraud-covid" target="_blank" >face criminal charges</a>. But the news also comes as federal prosecutors here have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >grappled with a scandal</a> that’s rippled through the city’s courthouse and led to the dismissal of charges against two of Ahmed’s co-defendants.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Sharon Johnson Coleman denied Ahmed’s bid for similar relief only two weeks ago — but she said she’d be willing to reconsider if Ahmed “submits to the court’s jurisdiction.”</p><p>Ahmed now appears to be taking her up on her offer, though his attorneys have yet to renew their request.</p><p>Prosecutors told the judge they’d only learned the news Wednesday morning.</p><p>Ahmed is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2024/07/12/loretto-hospital-cfo-15-million-embezzlement" target="_blank" >charged in two indictments</a> with defrauding millions of dollars out of Loretto hospital and the federal government. Both cases were led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Sheri Mecklenburg, the prosecutor at the center of the so-called “Broadview Six” scandal.</p><p>The “Broadview Six” conspiracy case, brought against six Operation Midway Blitz protesters, collapsed in late May over revelations of apparent misconduct by Mecklenburg before grand jurors.</p><p>Similar allegations soon surfaced about Mecklenburg’s conduct in the prosecution of Ahmed and others. Coleman in June threatened to hold a hearing over the allegations, but the feds avoided it by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/11/broadview-six-grand-jury-misconduct-federal-prosecutors-drop-charges-loretto-hospital-covid-fraud" target="_blank" >permanently dropping</a> charges against two other defendants.</p><p>Still, Coleman warned prosecutors then to “make sure that your boss understands," a reference to embattled <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/05/28/broadview-six-juliana-stratton-lori-lightfoot-andrew-boutros" target="_blank" >Chicago U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros</a>.</p><p>“That evidentiary hearing thing — it’s still a possibility. I’m not saying that’s over with, at least in this room,” Coleman told them.</p><p><i>This is a developing story. Check back for updates.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/01/28/ex-loretto-hospital-exec-accused-of-defrauding-feds-through-covid-19-testing-scheme-arrested-in-serbia" target="_blank" >Ex-Loretto Hospital exec accused of defrauding feds through COVID-19 testing scheme arrested in Serbia</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/26/broadview-six-loretto-hosptial-ice-sheri-mecklenburg-andrew-boutros" target="_blank" >Loretto exec’s fraud case now in jeopardy as ‘Broadview 6’ prosecutor faces scrutiny over alleged misconduct</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/11/broadview-six-grand-jury-misconduct-federal-prosecutors-drop-charges-loretto-hospital-covid-fraud" target="_blank" >After judge threatens hearing over grand jury misconduct, feds drop charges in case tied to Loretto exec</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Bears coach Ben Johnson still 'yells and curses' at QB Caleb Williams, but they're connecting much better
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach Ben Johnson was so hard on quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a> last season that at one point Williams worried that his coach didn't like him.</p><p>Nothing has changed in the way Johnson talks to him. Williams just understands it better.</p><p>"We have a real common goal, and it's to find a way to make the Chicago Bears champions," he said Wednesday after the team's first practice of training camp, a light session that lasted about an hour and a half. "Everything he says to me, I'll do it at 200% and won't look back... If he yells and curses at me or anything like that, I know it's for the greater good of the team."</p><p>Johnson's mandate that Williams completes 70% of his passes, both in practices and games, is part of that. After finishing last in the NFL at 58.1% last season, he needs to gain a lot of ground.</p><p>Williams struggled with throwing accuracy as a rookie, too, at just 62.5% and seemed perplexed by the dropoff from how he played at USC. With Johnson, there's a much clearer picture of why he's had trouble and what needs to be corrected.</p><p>Amid that process, the Bears want Williams to keep the qualities that make him a unique talent: his speed, his elusiveness in the pocket to extend plays and the unorthodox throws that delivered big results last season.</p><p>"Just hit the easy ones when they’re there," Williams said. "Be in rhythm with myself. Be confident in my guys. Be confident within the play. Deliver a good ball. Deliver a catchable ball. And then from there, when things happen, I put on the cape and do my thing, but it’s not something that needs to be on or showing until the moment shows up.”</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Rep. Delia Ramirez taking medical leave during August recess to recover from surgical procedure
entries.summary: <p>Illinois Congresswoman Delia Ramirez on Wednesday said she's taking several weeks off — during the congressional recess — to recover from a "time-sensitive" surgical procedure.</p><p>The Chicago Democrat said she was disclosing the medical matter, "acknowledging the American people's growing distrust in our public officials." </p><p>"That’s why I am sharing that I will be taking a several-week-long planned leave over the August recess to recover from a time-sensitive and medically required surgical procedure," Ramirez said in a statement. She did not disclose further details of the medical treatment. </p><p>The U.S. House has been in recess since July 23 and plans to return to session on Aug. 31. Ramirez, 43, said her medical procedure will coincide with the recess, and while her offices remain closed until Aug. 3 for the recess break, they will reopen on Aug. 4. </p><p>"As I begin my leave this week, I recognize the privilege I have to receive comprehensive healthcare and the ability to take time off to recover.," Ramirez said in the statement. "Today, many working families struggle to afford insurance while balancing multiple jobs. Thousands of women — especially women of color — are being denied reproductive care, whether it is because they live in restrictive states or because they are in inhumane ICE detention."</p><p>Ramirez won the 3rd Congressional District House seat in 2022, defeating Ald. Gilbert Villegas (36th) and two other challengers, and she easily won reelection in 2024. Ramirez became the first Guatemalan American elected to the state legislature in 2018.</p><p>Ramirez's disclosure comes as U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, 84, remains at a rehabilitation facility, where he is undergoing physical therapy. The Kentucky senator was hospitalized on June 14 and disclosed a month later that he suffered a fall and later contracted a mild case of pneumonia.</p><p>Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear on Tuesday sent a letter to McConnell asking him to prove that he is fit to continue serving or resign from office. The governor had first urged the former Senate majority leader in early July to release more information about his condition after weeks of silence — and amid rampant speculation about his condition. McConnell first released a photo on July 12 to provide an update on his health. </p><p>McConnell has missed 38 votes on the Senate floor since his hospitalization. </p>
entries.author: Tina Sfondeles

entries.title: Mayor makes a last appointment to Chicago school board, choosing leader on school integration plan
entries.summary: <p>Connie Anderson will fill a vacancy on Chicago’s school board representing the city’s Far South Side, Mayor Brandon Johnson’s office announced Wednesday.</p><p>That means Anderson will get to serve for a few months in the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/05/26/51-candidates-are-running-for-chicagos-first-fully-elected-school-board" target="_blank" ><u>seat she’s seeking in November</u></a>, when Chicagoans will vote for all 21 members of the school board for the first time. She’s still <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2026/07/28/at-least-5-chicago-school-board-races-to-be-uncontested-as-another-candidate-kicked-off-ballot" target="_blank" ><u>facing a challenge to her candidacy</u></a>, which will likely be decided by mid-August. There is one other candidate in that race and one expected write-in.</p><p>Anderson will likely be the last, or one of the last, members ever appointed to the school board.</p><p>She will represent District 10B, a seat previously held by Olga Bautista, <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/03/04/chicago-public-schools-board-vice-president-olga-bautista-steps-down/" target="_blank" ><u>who stepped down in March</u></a>.</p><p>In a news release, the mayor’s office praised Anderson as a respected community leader and education advocate who has worked with Chicago Public Schools on science and technology initiatives. She helped develop student robotics teams in CPS and served for a dozen years as a member of the Friends of Ogden parent group, which helps raise money for the school.</p><p>The mayor’s office noted that Anderson played a key role in the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2018/09/05/two-schools-at-opposite-ends-of-income-divide-become-one" target="_blank" ><u>controversial 2018 merger</u></a> of two North Side schools, Ogden International School and Jenner Academy of the Arts. The complex integration plan meant bridging racial and class divides between the whiter, more affluent student body at Ogden and the Black students from lower-income families at Jenner, which had historically served children living in Cabrini-Green’s public housing.</p><p>“As a parent of CPS graduates, this work is deeply personal to me and I look forward to bringing my experience in education, entrepreneurship, and community engagement to support the continued success of our students,” Anderson said in a statement.</p>

entries.title: Con el bate a todo, el jugador suplente Pedro Ramírez impresiona a los Cubs con sus contribuciones
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS — La experiencia de <b>Pedro Ramírez</b> ha sido positiva para los <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a>.</p><p>El joven jugador de cuadro ha impresionado a la directiva en su primera toma de contacto con las Grandes Ligas esta temporada, y se ha acomodado bien como reserva.</p><p>Ramírez, uno de los prospectos mejor valorados de los Cubs al inicio de la temporada, ha logrado mantenerse efectivo pese a no jugar todos los días.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-620000" name="module-620000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Antes del juego del lunes, acumulaba una racha de siete partidos sin ser eliminado, en los que bateó .440 y sumó cuatro actuaciones con múltiples imparables.</p><p>"Ha manejado muy bien muchas de estas situaciones, como no jugar todos los días y aun así ser productivo", dijo la semana pasada el mánager <b>Craig Counsell</b>. "Y defensivamente también ha estado muy bien, especialmente en la antesala. Ha sido excelente. Hay mucho que gusta”.</p><p>"Para un muchacho de 22 años que sube y juega de forma esporádica y está en el banquillo y aun así contribuye, ha sido divertido verlo", agregó.</p><p>El tiempo de juego limitado a veces puede jugar en contra de un pelotero, y los Cubs han manifestado su intención de rotar a jóvenes como el jardinero <b>Kevin Alcántara</b>, el jugador de cuadro <b>James Triantos</b> y el receptor/designado <b>Moisés Ballesteros</b> en diferentes plazas del roster. Las etapas en las Grandes Ligas han incluido —y seguirán incluyendo— bajar al equipo menor para evitar oxidarse en el banquillo.</p><p>Sin embargo, Ramírez no se ha oxidado. Llegó al partido del lunes con un promedio de bateo de .305 y un OPS plus de 122. Eso significa que ha sido un 22% más productivo que el bateador promedio de las Grandes Ligas, un grupo que incluye a muchos jugadores con mucha más experiencia en las mayores.</p><p>Mientras los Cubs trazan su futuro —y el presidente Jed Hoyer se pone a trabajar de cara a la fecha límite de cambios, con <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/24/cubs-trade-rumors-mlb-trade-deadline-top-prospects-james-triantos-pedro-ramirez-matt-shaw-jed-hoyer" target="_blank" >los jóvenes como parte de la ecuación</a>—, Ramírez ha dejado una impresión inicial muy positiva.</p><p>"Hemos hablado de no jugar", dijo Counsell. "[Antes del receso del Juego de Estrellas] en Cincinnati estuvimos en un tramo en el que no estaba jugando tanto... Es la primera vez que le pasa. Para tipos como Pedro —tienes 22 años y ya estás en las Grandes Ligas—, nunca antes habías dejado de ir al campo ni de preguntarte si estarías en la alineación. Jugabas todos los días”.</p><p>"Tuvimos una buena conversación al respecto. Pero él entiende todo eso. Tiene un marco de referencia muy bueno. Su trabajo en ese tipo de cosas ha sido el adecuado. Simplemente va por delante. Está adelantado en cómo afrontar las situaciones, y eso es realmente impresionante", aseguró</p><h3>Noches de cuatro imparables</h3><p>El antesalista <b>Alex Bregman</b> y el intermedista <b>Nico Hoerner</b> conectaron sendos juegos de cuatro imparables en la victoria de los Cubs por 7-3 el lunes ante los Cardinals.</p><p>Cada uno conectó un jonrón; Bregman añadió dos dobles, dos carreras impulsadas y tres carreras anotadas. Hoerner tuvo cuatro carreras impulsadas y dos anotadas.</p><p>Bregman, que todavía intenta recuperar la consistencia ofensiva, elevó su promedio de bateo en julio de .192 a .231. Hoerner, por su parte, desapareció la pelota por primera vez desde el 21 de abril, rompiendo una racha de 80 partidos sin jonrón.</p><h3>El regreso de Cabrera</h3><p>El derecho <b>Edward Cabrera</b> está cerca de iniciar una asignación de rehabilitación con las menores tras una distensión en el isquiotibial que lo ha dejado fuera durante un mes.</p><p>Cabrera lanzará el viernes en Triple-A Iowa en la primera de tres salidas de rehabilitación planificadas. Si todo sale bien, tendría previsto regresar a la rotación a mediados de agosto.</p><p>Aunque el regreso de Cabrera será importante para una rotación que aún lidia con los efectos de una avalancha de lesiones, todavía no ha entregado el tipo de resultados que los Cubs esperaban cuando lo adquirieron en un intercambio de temporada baja con los Marlins. Tiene una efectividad de 5.10 en 14 aperturas.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Bears DE Montez Sweat back from illness
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> defensive end Montez Sweat's illness, as it turns out, cost him just 24 hours.</p><p>One day after the Bears put their best defensive end on the Non-Football Illness list, they removed him from it <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/07/29/bears-training-camp-report-practice-no-1-wednesday-halas-hall-luther-burden-tory-taylor-nfl" target="_blank" >Wednesday afternoon</a>. In between, he missed the team's first training camp practice of the year, a brief occasion on the backfields at Halas Hall. Sweat is expected to participate in Thursday morning's practice.</p><p>Sweat was never expected to miss serious time, but his return is good news nonetheless, particularly after the Bears went all offseason without adding significant edge rushers in free agency, trades or the draft. Sweat is coming off of one of the best seasons of his career, a 10-sack showing. The Bears had little production opposite Sweat short of a late surge by Austin Booker after he returned from injury. </p><p>On Tuesday, general manager Ryan Poles said he wanted to "see [Sweat] continue to improve and take what he did last year and add to that."</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Former Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan asks U.S. Supreme Court to hear his corruption case
entries.summary: <p>Former Illinois House Speaker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/madigan-trial-news" target="_blank" >Michael J. Madigan</a> took the long-awaited step Wednesday of asking the nation’s highest court to hear an appeal of the historic corruption conviction that could keep him behind bars until he is nearly 90 years old.</p><p>The move comes three months after the federal appeals court in Chicago <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/madigan-trial-news/2026/04/27/illinois-madigan-comed-corruption-speaker-house" target="_blank" >upheld Madigan’s</a> February 2025 conviction, finding that trial evidence “exposed a sustained and concealed arrangement to exchange enormous political influence within the Illinois General Assembly for over $3 million of benefit for political allies.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/madigan-trial-news/mike-madigan-guilty-verdict" >Once a political giant, Madigan now a convicted felon and likely prison inmate — but not a racketeer</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Madigan’s lawyers want the U.S. Supreme Court to grapple with key legal questions from his case, including when a public official acts “corruptly” and whether an alleged promise to make a job recommendation qualifies as an “official act.”</p><p>“The novel bribery theories the government zealously pursued against Speaker Madigan stretch federal bribery law in ways that threaten to criminalize and chill lawful interactions between state and local officials and their constituents,” Madigan’s lawyers told the justices in their petition.</p><p>Madigan’s legal team includes Lisa Blatt, a well-known high court litigator who claims an 82% win rate before the Supreme Court. She <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/madigan-trial-news/2026/04/09/madigan-corruption-conviction-appeal-federal-7th-circuit" target="_blank" >attended arguments</a> in Madigan’s case before the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in April.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in April.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Supreme Court only takes a fraction of the cases presented to it, making Madigan's petition a long shot. But the high court has already upended Madigan's case once. In June 2024, it used a separate case to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials/2024/06/26/supreme-court-snyder-ruling-madigan-corruption" target="_blank" >limit the feds’ use</a> of a bribery law at the center of Madigan's prosecution. The justices also debated the meaning of the word "corruptly" during arguments but never defined it.</p><p>A federal jury in February 2025 convicted Madigan, now 84, of a bribery conspiracy, wire fraud and other crimes. U.S. District Judge John<b> </b>Blakey<b> </b>handed Madigan a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/06/13/mike-madigan-sentencing-hearing" target="_blank" >7½-year prison sentence</a> four months later, finding that Madigan lied to the jury <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/madigan-trial-news/2025/01/07/michael-madigan-will-testify-own-defense-corruption-trial" target="_blank" >when he testified</a> in his own defense.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/madigan-trial-news/2025/10/13/former-illinois-house-speaker-michael-madigan-is-in-prison" target="_blank" >Madigan then surrendered</a><b> </b>to a minimum-security prison camp in West Virginia last October.</p><p>The former speaker’s conviction centered on two schemes. In one, ComEd paid five Madigan allies $1.3 million over eight years so Madigan would look more favorably at the utility’s legislation. The money was funneled through third-party firms,<b> </b>and the recipients did hardly any work for ComEd.</p><p>The utility also paid $1.8 million to the Reyes Kurson law firm as part of the conspiracy.</p><p>The other scheme involved a deal to have then-Chicago Ald. Danny Solis<b> </b>installed on a state board in exchange for Solis’ help landing private business for Madigan’s tax appeal law firm. Solis had been working undercover for the FBI at the time, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials/2025/04/04/danny-solis-federal-prosecutors-bribery-dirksen-courthouse" target="_blank" >in a bid to avoid prison</a> for his own alleged wrongdoing.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f10000" name="image-f10000"></a> <picture entries.title: TF North basketball coach and former Simeon star Tim Bankston found fatally shot in Auburn Gresham home
entries.summary: <p>Tim Bankston, a South Side basketball legend at Simeon and current boys basketball coach at Thornton Fractional North High School in Calumet City, was found fatally shot Wednesday morning inside a home in Auburn Gresham on the South Side, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Bankston, 60, was found unresponsive with a gunshot wound to his abdomen around 10 a.m. in the 7600 block of South Emerald Avenue, police said in a statement. He was pronounced dead at the scene.</p><p>Police said no one else was injured and reported no arrests. No additional details were released.</p><p>A large crowd of family, former Simeon teammates and former players gathered on Emerald to mourn Bankston and support each other Wednesday afternoon.</p><div Ward Ald. David Moore said. "The police had not put out the report to me yet. I was on my way back home and my friend told me he was gone. I cannot believe this. It just brings back all the things with [Ben] "Benji" [Wilson]. It was not supposed to go like this. He was not supposed to go like this."</p><p>Bankston was a Simeon teammate of Wilson, who was fatally shot on the South Side in November of 1984, shortly before his senior basketball season was about to begin. Wilson was the top-rated player in the country. </p><p>"We don’t know what happened yet," Sean Wright, a relative of Bankston, said. "They said they found my brother’s body and to come as fast as you can. From what the officer said, it looked like he had been laying there overnight."</p><p>Bankston led Simeon to the state title in 1984, after which he played one year at Bradley and two years at Loyola. He was inducted into the Illinois Basketball Coaches Hall of Fame as a player and has been the head coach at TF North since 2002. Bankston was married and had three children.</p><p>"He always spoke his mind," said Mac Elem, who played for Bankston at TF North in 2012. "He was the best coach on and off the court I ever had. He taught you how to be a man and how to run a team. He wasn’t just a coach. He was family, like an uncle. He made an impact on a lot of people, a lot of my friends."</p><p><i>This is a developing story. entries.title: City Council urged to postpone police superintendent search until after mayoral election
entries.summary: <p>A key member of a Chicago police oversight body urged the City Council Wednesday to postpone <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/02/chicago-police-superintendent-larry-snelling-retirement-search-for-replacement" >the search for a permanent replacement</a> for retired Police Supt. Larry Snelling until after the mayoral election.</p><p>As president of the Community Commission for Public Safety and Accountability, Anthony Driver led the nationwide search that culminated in Mayor Brandon Johnson’s selection of Snelling. Driver stepped down as president to mount what turned out to be a losing race for Congress, but he is still a commission member involved in the search for Snelling’s replacement.</p><p>In a letter to City Council members Wednesday, Driver asked that the Nov. 12 deadline for the commission to complete a nationwide search, interview candidates and present the names of three finalists to Johnson be put off until spring — after Chicagoans choose their next mayor.</p><p>“My concern is rooted entirely in one objective: ensuring that Chicago attracts the strongest possible pool of candidates for one of the most important public safety positions in the country,” Driver wrote. “At a time when Chicago is experiencing historic reductions in homicides and violent crime, this process is simply too important to get wrong.”</p><p>Johnson has not yet decided whether to wage what will almost certainly be an uphill battle for reelection or walk away after a single term. </p><p>But he has already rejected the call by his Council opposition to allow the winner of the 2027 mayoral election to select Snelling’s replacement.</p><p>”Look, there’s a process. There’s a law that places us on a pretty strict timeline," Johnson told WBEZ’s Sasha-Ann Simons on the most recent installment of "Ask the Mayor." "To cut off democracy — and democracy has to wait based upon a political cycle or calendar? I don’t find that to be a reasonable way to govern.</p><p>“What is that suggesting? That I’m not going to be here? So we’re making decisions again based upon chance or lots? I’m just going to be very direct here. I find that to be absolutely ridiculous — insulting to the people of Chicago. So we should stop a process based upon someone’s political calendar? That is old-school-style governance, and that’s what got us into this mess. I’m here to clean it up.”</p><p> Driver stressed that his call for a delayed timeline is “not a political argument, nor is it an indictment of the current mayor, civilian oversight or the ordinance itself.”</p><p>His only purpose in urging the Council to extend the Nov.12 deadline until "next spring after Chicago has certainty regarding its executive leadership" is to convince "the best candidates available" that it's worth the "professional risk that accompanies a confidential national search." </p><p>"We know that this concern is on the minds of potential candidates. For some of the very leaders we most hope to recruit, the combination may be enough to discourage them from applying at all," he wrote.</p><p>Ald. Matt O’Shea (19th), whose Far Southwest Side ward is home to scores of Chicago police officers, told the Chicago Sun-Times on the day after Snelling’s retirement announcement that it made no sense to let Johnson, whom he called a "lame-duck mayor," choose the next superintendent before the mayoral election.</p><p>Now that Driver, who led the search that produced "the best superintendent we've had in the modern era" is saying "let's pump the brakes," O'Shea said the Council should "be doing just that."</p><p>"We need to get this right. We need to get the most talented people to apply for this position. Chicago needs it. Chicago deserves it," O'Shea said Wednesday. "We should slow down this process and make sure that we're coming up with the best possible candidates to lead the third-largest police department in our country."</p><p>Police Committee Chair Chris Taliaferro (29th) urged the commission to forge ahead with the search.</p><p>“Why would we extend the process if there’s not a need to extend the process? If we get 100 qualified applicants over the next 30 days, why is there a need to extend it beyond 120 days other than for political reasons?” Taliaferro said.</p><p>He likened the calls for a pre-emptive delay to the U.S. Senate’s decision to block then-President Barack Obama’s appointment of Merrick Garland in 2016 to fill a vacancy on the U.S. Supreme Court.</p><p>“They said he had less [than] a year to serve in his presidency. I don’t think that is a valid reason to deny this mayor an opportunity to appoint a superintendent of police,” Taliaferro said.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p>If the Council agrees to follow Driver’s suggestion, it wouldn’t be the first time that the search for a new Chicago police superintendent was altered.</p><p>In 2016, then-Mayor Rahm Emanuel rejected the three finalists presented to him by then-Police Board President Lori Lightfoot. At Emanuel’s request, the City Council then changed the law that required a second nationwide search, allowing Emanuel to appoint Eddie Johnson.</p>

entries.title: Glen Hansard, Irish singer with deep roots in Chicago, dies at 56
entries.summary: <p>Glen Hansard, the beloved Irish musician who had a special connection to Chicago, died early Wednesday in Ireland after a motorcycle accident.</p><p>Hansard was killed in a single-vehicle crash in his home city of Dublin, <a class="Link" href="https://www.rte.ie/news/ireland/2026/0729/1585555-glen-hansard-death/" target="_blank" >according to RTE</a>, Ireland's public broadcasting service. He was 56.</p><p>ATC management, which represented Hansard, posted to Facebook Wednesday morning: "With broken hearts we announce the passing of Glen Hansard in the early hours of this morning. We are still dealing with the shock of it all, so we kindly ask that the privacy of Glen’s family, colleagues and friends is respected at this difficult time."</p><p>The Irish musician lived in the North Center neighborhood in the early 2000s.</p><p>“It was a special time for us, and Chicago became my home,” Hansard said March 31 while <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/04/01/review-glen-hansard-chicago-show-evanston-space" target="_blank" >performing at Space in Evanston</a>.</p><p>During his time living here, Hansard and his band, The Frames, worked with famed audio engineer Steve Albini, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2024/05/08/steve-albini-dead-legendary-rock-underground-pioneer-was-61-obituary" >who died in 2024</a>, at his Electrical Audio studio on West Belmont in the Avondale neighborhood.</p><p>Chicago native Rob Bochnik became Hansard's longtime guitarist.</p><p>Michael Cameron, owner of Uncommon Ground, a North Side restaurant and music venue, said he invited Hansard to perform a solo show at his venue in the late 1990s to introduce him to people from Chicago's music industry, who packed his small 50-seat venue.</p><p>The idea was the brainchild of Zoran Orlic, a friend and Chicago-area music photographer who was traveling with The Frames.</p><p>Cameron became good friends with Hansard, and was hoping Hansard would be a surprise guest this Saturday at a show that would have featured a number of Chicago musicians playing Hansard's music as part of a celebration of Uncommon Ground's 35th anniversary.</p><p>"The logistics just didn't make sense so he couldn't come. But I had a reminder in my phone to reach out to him today and have him send a video message we could play at the show. But when I woke up this morning, my phone was blowing up and we learned what happened, and my wife and I both were sobbing."</p><p>Several of the musicians slated to take the stage have played with Hansard and were his friends, Cameron said.</p><p>"We're going to pause that show for now. Everything is just too raw. Everyone is devastated, so we'll give it a day or two and I'll reach back out to everyone and see what they want to do," he said.</p><p>Hansard dropped out of school at 13 to begin busking on the streets of his hometown of Dublin. He formed The Frames in 1990.</p><p>His career was thrust to new heights following the 2007 release of the film "Once," which starred Hansard and Czech singer Markéta Irglová as struggling musicians.</p><p>The song "Falling Slowly" from the movie's soundtrack won them the 2008 Academy Award for Best Original Song, the film was adapted into a Tony Award-winning stage musical, and Hansard and Irglová, who for a time had a real-life romantic relationship, performed as Swell Season at venues across the world, including Chicago.</p><p></p><p>He <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/3/13/22975587/swell-season-review-chicago-glen-hansard-marketa-irglova-conceert-cadillac-palace-tour-ukraine" target="_blank" >reunited with Irglova</a> for an emotional show at Cadillac Palace Theatre in 2022. They also performed as Swell Season in July 2025 at the Auditorium Theatre.</p><p>In 2024, he played the Salt Shed and later that year he performed at Wrigley Field as an opener for Pearl Jam. Hansard would also moonlight as one of the Earthlings in Eddie Vedder’s solo project.</p><p>The Frames played all over Chicago at venues including Metro, Schubas and even the old Abbey Pub in 2002.</p><p>Bruce Finkelman, managing partner of 16 on Center, which operates a number of music venues, including Space, Thalia Hall and the Salt Shed, said Wednesday that Hansard had a naturally friendly and warming presence.</p><p>"He was well loved in the Chicago music scene, and for all intents and purposes, it felt like he was part of it," Finkelman said, noting that Hansard's previous longtime manager was Chicagoan Howard Greynold.</p><p>Hansard was also an investor in Thalia Hall, a music venue in Pilsen that opened in 2013, Finkelman said.</p><p>One of Hansard's first connections to Chicago was through the late folk musician Jason Molina, who lived in Chicago and performed as Songs: Ohia.</p><p>The way the two men met is a tale from a different era, Hansard told NPR Music in 2015.</p><p>Hansard was touring with The Frames when he bought a Songs: Ohia album in Alabama, listened to it for the rest of the tour and wrote a letter to the P.O. Box he saw on the packaging.</p><p>"I didn't even know if this band existed anymore. I wasn't sure if it was a current band, if it was an old band — because it was before the days of being able to look it all up," Hansard told NPR Music. "And I wrote the letter to this address, saying, 'If you ever wanted to tour in Ireland, I would be so happy to host you with my own band.' And he got back! He said, 'Hello, I'm Jason, it's my record you bought — and yeah, let's do it.'"</p>

entries.title: What to know after tornadoes tore through Chicago area suburbs
entries.summary: <p>Powerful storms that swept across the Chicago area Monday left neighborhoods in the south suburbs picking up the pieces after five tornadoes touched down — damaging homes, uprooting trees and adding to what has already been an active tornado season in Illinois.</p><p>An EF-1 tornado with peak winds of 110 mph impacted Lansing, according to the National Weather Service. The fifth tornado, an EF-0 that touched down just south of Wheaton College, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/29/5th-tornado-confirmed-monday-storms-national-weather-service" >was confirmed only Wednesday</a>.</p><p>Rob Griffin, a Lansing resident, told the Sun-Times he underestimated the severity of the storm that hit his far south suburb.</p><p>"Even though they had the sirens on and sent alerts to our phones, I kind of ignored it because most times they do that as more of a warning," Griffin said. "So I didn’t heed the warning.”</p><p>As tornado season continues to surge across Illinois, here's what you need to know.</p><h3><b>What happened during Monday’s storms?</b></h3><p>Five powerful storms swept across the Chicago area Monday according to the National Weather Service, causing significant damage to homes and trees. They also brought significant rainfall, with McCook Reservoir nearing capacity. It was just the lastest episode in what already has been an active tornado season in Illinois.</p><p>For Lansing resident Abo Lorebelo, the storm was unlike anything he had experienced in the four years he's lived there. He and his family sheltered in their basement while the tornado moved through, but their home still suffered major roof damage.</p><h3><b>Why are there so many tornadoes in Illinois this year?</b></h3><p>So far this year, Illinois has experienced a record number of tornadoes.</p><p>Meteorologists say multiple rounds of severe weather this spring and summer have contributed to the elevated tornado count.</p><p>Before Monday's storms, the weather service estimated the state already had recorded 183 tornadoes, far surpassing the previous record of 142 tornadoes, set in 2024. The total is expected to change as the weather service routinely updates their storm survey database.</p><h3><b>Can tornadoes happen in the Chicago area?</b></h3><p>Yes, and they have.</p><p>While many people associate tornadoes with rural communities, Monday’s storms served as another reminder that tornadoes can impact communities throughout Chicago and its suburbs.</p><p>Victor Gensini, director of Northern Illinois University’s Center for Interdisciplinary Research on Convective Storms, has previously warned residents never to assume tornadoes cannot hit densely populated areas.</p><h3><b>What should I do after a tornado alert?</b></h3><p>Illinois State Climatologist Trent Ford said every Midwesterner should have the proper plans in place in the event of severe weather warnings. Making sure that your family is safe and together and knows what to do. Things like going down into the basement (if you have one) and keeping your phone and other electronic items charged in case of outages. All that, and make sure to follow messaging from the National Weather Service,.</p><p>Some residents admitted they, like Griffin in Lansing, underestimated Monday's storm despite emergency alerts being sent to mobile phones and the blaring of tornado sirens.</p><p>"I think they're doing a good job of warning us," said Griffin, who lost nearly all his roof during the storm. "Hopefully we, as citizens, will take heed to that."</p><h3><b>Are tornadoes becoming more common in Illinois?</b></h3><p>To see just how active the 2026 tornado season has been, consider this.</p><p>The University of Illinois climatologist's office added up how many tornadoes occurred in the state in July over the 70-year span from 1950-2020. The answer: 181.</p><p>That's 181, total. Over all 70 years.</p><p>With this year’s statewide tally, Illinois already has exceeded that total in less than a year. </p><p>So while tornado activity can change from year to year, this year that activity has reached the highest point in recent years.</p><p>Still, it doesn't mean Illinois is the new Tornado Alley. Yet.</p><p>That phrase is a “media colloquialism” coined in the early 1950s and is in no way an official designation, Gensini has previously cautioned the Sun-Times.</p><p>“If I ask 100 of my meteorology friends to define" what Tornado Alley is, he said, "they’d each have a different answer."</p><p>According to some definitions, Illinois actually been considered part of Tornado Alley for some time. Initially, the nickname applied to southwestern states ravaged by twisters in the last century, such as Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas.</p><h3><b>Is climate change causing more tornadoes?</b></h3><p>The answer isn't straightforward.</p><p>Ford told the Sun-Times warmer temperatures and increased moisture in the atmosphere can create environments that favor stronger thunderstorms.</p><p>However, researchers say the relationship between climate change and tornadoes themselves remains less certain.</p><p>Ford said a warmer, more humid climate may be contributing to more environments favorable for severe storms, though scientists are still studying exactly how those conditions affect tornado frequency.</p><h3><b>What happens next?</b></h3><p>The National Weather Service will continue surveying storm damage across the region throughout the week to determine the final strength and paths of Monday’s tornadoes.</p><p>As cleanup continues, many Lansing residents say the storm has changed how they will respond the next time severe weather warnings are issued. For Griffin and others across the south suburbs, Monday’s storms were a reminder that preparation and taking warnings seriously can make a difference when severe weather strikes.</p><p><i>Contributing: Brett Chase</i></p>

entries.title: Trade chip or future piece? Right now, Pedro Ramirez happy to help Cubs: ‘It’s always been a dream of mine’
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS – In five of his last eight games coming into Wednesday, <b>Pedro Ramirez</b> collected multiple hits.</p><p>Despite sporadic playing time, the Cubs’ rookie infielder was batting .467 with a 1.133 OPS during an eight-game hitting streak.</p><p>Ramirez has taken advantage of an opportunity and stuck around as a positive contributor on a Cubs team with one of the best records in baseball and championship-level expectations.</p><p>“It’s always been a dream of mine to be on a competitive team,” Ramirez said Wednesday through an interpreter. “You go out there and you play with that passion. You have that mindset of: ‘We have to win. We’re going to win.’ It’s really exciting to be part of that.</p><p>“It’s always been my aspiration, my goal, to be part of a group like that, a competitive group.”</p><p>Ramirez is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/27/cubs-pedro-ramirez-bench-player-jed-hoyer-craig-counsell-mlb-trade-deadline-edward-cabrera-injury-andrew-wantz" >undoubtedly making an impact</a>. But has he made a big enough impact that he’s played his way into a trade conversation or two ahead of Monday’s trade deadline?</p><p>As a young player – he’s graduated from prospect status but was among the Cubs’ highest rated prospects earlier this year – he’s at least a sensible candidate to be mentioned as <b>Jed Hoyer</b>’s front office <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/17/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-starting-pitching-jed-hoyer-front-office" >pursues impact pitching</a> to best equip the roster for a deep playoff run.</p><p>Hoyer <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2025/07/31/2025-trade-deadline-cubs-prez-jed-hoyer-balks-at-asking-price-for-frontline-starter-adds-four-players" >balked at the price of pitching</a> at last year’s deadline, opting against mortgaging the future. After pitching-depth issues helped the Cubs make an earlier-than-hoped postseason exit, Hoyer traded prospect <b>Owen Caissie</b> for righty <b>Edward Cabrera</b> in the offseason.</p><p>If the Cubs are to avoid the same fate this October, it would figure to require <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/24/cubs-trade-rumors-mlb-trade-deadline-top-prospects-james-triantos-pedro-ramirez-matt-shaw-jed-hoyer" >parting with young players of note</a>.</p><p>Fans have speculated that Ramirez could be among the most attractive, and his performance has backed up that idea.</p><p>“It’s awesome for him to be in there and produce,” left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b> said. “He’s a good player. He’s got a lot of great tools that you see on display. He’s a gamer.”</p><p>Apart from the trade talk, Ramirez has proven himself worthy of consideration to play a featured role for the Cubs in the future.</p><p>But with infielders <b>Nico Hoerner</b>, <b>Alex Bregman</b> and <b>Dansby Swanson</b> signed to big-money, long-term contracts, it’s a wonder how Ramirez would fit into the puzzle.</p><p>The guys helping him learn as a young player – “watching them has really helped me a lot with my defense,” he said – could prevent him from finding regular playing time, perhaps a factor in any decision to use him as a trade chip this summer.</p><p>But Hoyer cautioned against assuming youngsters would be heading out the door.</p><p>“The players that people were talking about as trade chips at this point, those are the players that next year may be impacting us,” Hoyer said. “You always have to keep that in mind.”</p><p><b>Milner on the mound</b></p><p>Lefty reliever <b>Hoby Milner</b>, working back after a late-June appendectomy, threw a 1-2-3 inning as part of a minor league rehab assignment Wednesday at Triple-A Iowa.</p><p>Manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said Milner will make another rehab appearance before returning to the big league team.</p><p><b>Starting-pitcher swap</b></p><p>The Cubs will throw righty <b>Javier Assad</b> against the Cardinals on Thursday, moving lefty <b>Shota Imanaga</b>, the previously announced probable starter, to Friday’s series-opener against the Yankees, opting to get the southpaw an extra day of rest.</p><p><b>Bullpen move</b></p><p>The Cubs swapped pitchers in their ‘pen Wednesday, bringing right-hander <b>Jake Woodford</b> up from Triple-A Iowa and designating righty <b>Andrew Wantz</b> for assignment.</p><p><b>Time change</b></p><p>The Cubs’ Aug. 30 game against the Reds has a new start time of 6:20 p.m. to accommodate NBC’s “Sunday Night Baseball” broadcast.</p>
