entries.title: White Sox righty Sean Burke delivering on personal pact during red-hot run
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> right-hander Sean Burke doesn’t come off as someone who’s easily angered. He looks mild-mannered and sounds soft-spoken.</p><p>But after his first two starts of June, Burke was simmering. He lasted no longer than 4⅓ innings in either, and he walked five in both.</p><p>He had entered the season aiming to pound the strike zone and get ahead of hitters, neither of which he did enough last season. He vowed this year would be different, no matter what.</p><p>“If I’m getting hit around the yard for 15 hits, I’m still going to keep making you beat me in the zone,” Burke told the Sun-Times this week. “And those two starts, I really hadn’t been in the zone. I went against my pact to myself.”</p><p>His third start that month came in New York against the Yankees, who had just pummeled the Sox 12-2 and 10-5. Burke followed opener Bryan Hudson, entering with two outs in the second inning and a 1-0 lead. He allowed a solo homer in the third, but that was it.</p><p>Burke went the rest of the way, giving up five hits and a walk and striking out eight, tying his then-season high, in the Sox’ 5-1 victory.</p><p>What changed?</p><p>“Honestly, I was just throwing pissed off,” he said. “Just throwing it as hard as I could in the zone, and I was able to get good results. I think [I showed] myself that’s how I need to be all the time. I can’t have those mental lapses of forgetting that.”</p><p>And he hasn’t. He’ll face the Yankees again Thursday on quite a run. In his last seven outings, beginning with that game at Yankee Stadium, Burke has a 1.61 ERA in 44⅔ innings with 57 strikeouts and only seven walks. He pitched without an opener in the last six — and he probably won’t need one again.</p><p>In the short time between last season and now, Burke thinks he has developed into more of a complete pitcher, which has sent his confidence soaring.</p><p>“I feel like I have more tools in my toolbox to get people out,” he said. “Last year at times I felt like I was kind of pigeonholed into throwing a certain pitch in a certain location to certain hitters.</p><p>“Now I feel like I [have] the ability to throw pitches to different quadrants, to shape breaking balls differently, to get ahead of guys in different ways and then finish guys in different ways, too. I feel like when I’m out there pitching, I’m able to process it a lot better.”</p><p>Burke credited Sox reliever Grant Taylor with helping him keep his delivery consistent. In 2024, they were roommates for a month while rehabbing injuries at the Sox’ complex in Arizona. In that time, they exchanged ideas of how to help the other perform better. The way Burke tells it, Taylor had a profound impact on him.</p><p>“Grant gave me a lot of ideas, just talking to him about what he feels in his delivery,” Burke said. “Obviously, you see the product he is now, but a lot of people didn’t see him when he was rehabbing on the back fields, sitting at 101 [mph]. He’s really advanced for his age for how he moves, how he takes care of his body.”</p><p>Taylor learned from Wes Johnson, his pitching coach at LSU. Johnson preached using a “water bag” to help stabilize his pitchers’ deliveries. It’s a large tube strapped to a pitcher’s back that rests behind the shoulders. The water inside helps a pitcher with their rotation.</p><p>“As you go through your motion, you can hear and feel the water slosh,” Taylor said. “When I was trying to do it, I’m trying to see how loud and how powerful I can feel the water slosh and go from one side to the other.</p><p>“That was something that me and [Burke] talked about, and he liked it. You're transferring more power from the ground up to your shoulders to get the rotation. It’s gotten bigger as the years have gone on.”</p><p>Never mind that Taylor was developing as a reliever and Burke as a starter. The goal for all pitchers is to repeat their delivery. The water bag helped Burke do that. But he still needed to learn to command his pitches. This season, it’s all coming together.</p><p>“The big thing I’ve seen from him is confidence and coming into his own with his own pitch plan,” Taylor said. “It’s been a lot of fun to watch. When we were rehabbing together, I was like, he’s going to be a really good big-leaguer. I think you saw that toward the end of last year, and then he’s just run away with it this year.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: 5th tornado confirmed from Monday's storms
entries.summary: <p>The National Weather Service on Wednesday afternoon confirmed another tornado from Monday’s storms, bringing the total to five.</p><p>The weather service said the EF-0 tornado touched down just south of Wheaton College with 75 mph winds surrounded by straight-line thunderstorm winds. Teams are still surveying damage and assessing data, according to a statement on social media.</p><p>“Widespread straight-line wind damage occurred from eastern Will/southern Cook into central Lake County [Indiana], in particular around the Beecher-Crete-Chicago Heights areas where winds likely exceeded 80 mph at times,” the service wrote on social media.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/28/storms-flooding-tornadoes-damage-worker-missing-power-outage" target="_blank" ><u>other four tornadoes</u></a> touched down in the south and west suburbs.</p><p>A tornado hit Lansing, and another that tore through Country Club Hills, Hazel Crest, Harvey and Homewood had gusts topping 110 miles an hour, according to the weather service. Two other confirmed tornadoes touched down in Glen Ellyn and Orland Park, each with winds reaching 85 mph.</p><p></p><p>Midway Airport recorded winds of 73 mph and O’Hare Airport saw 65 mph winds that night.</p><p>Further north in the Fox Cities region of Wisconsin, an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/28/wisconsin-tornado" target="_blank" ><u>EF-3 tornado touched down</u></a> around 1 p.m. and remained on the ground for more than 20 minutes, cutting a roughly 12-mile path of destruction, the National Weather Service reported. The area is about 100 miles northwest of Milwaukee.</p><p>It was the strongest to strike Outagamie and Winnebago counties since an EF4 touched down in April 1984, the weather service said.</p>

entries.title: Michigan State coach Pat Fitzgerald embracing his fresh start
entries.summary: <p>Pat Fitzgerald wears an emerald tie these days and ends his press conferences with an enthusiastic "Go Green!"</p><p>But his long, often successful tenure as a player and coach at Northwestern — which <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/northwestern-hazing-scandal" >ended in an abrupt and ugly manner</a> — still casts a long shadow.</p><p>It's been three years since Fitzgerald was fired by the university amid a hazing scandal and a year after he settled a lawsuit with the school, which said its investigation did not find any evidence that he knew of or condoned any hazing.</p><p>On Wednesday, Fitzgerald was back at Big Ten Media Days at the Hilton Chicago as the first-year coach at Michigan State. He's energized by the challenge of rebuilding a program that faded from relevance since the 2020 retirement of Mark D'Antonio.</p><p>But Fitzgerald prefers the term "rebirth" to "rebuild," and the former is also an apt descriptor for this stage of his coaching career.</p><p>What did he miss about coaching during his hiatus from the college game? He pushed back politely but firmly against the idea that he went away at all.</p><p>"I never left the game, for sure," Fitzgerald said.</p><p>He worked as a volunteer assistant at Loyola Academy where one of his sons (Ryan) quarterbacked a pair of state-champion teams before walking on at Iowa and another (Brendan) will be a senior receiver this fall. Fitzgerald also spent time at Iowa with longtime Hawkeyes coach Kirk Ferentz.</p><p>"I learned a lot," Fitzgerald said of his time at Loyola. "I became a better teacher. When you're teaching a young guy how to run a curl route and he's like, 'What is a curl?' Like what about the freshman or sophomore coaches here, what are you guys doing? Wait, I'm a volunteer dad, here to help."</p><p>Jokes aside, Fitzgerald's silver lining in the dark cloud of his Northwestern departure was that extra family time. That, and finding out who had his back.</p><p>"It's funny when issues arise and people run to you, you really find out who your friends are," he said. "I'm just really thankful for a great group of people that really were supportive. ... I think it's hardened my resolve and I'm just very thankful and grateful to be back in this role."</p><p>Calling himself "a Big Ten guy," Fitzgerald said Michigan State was on his short list of potential landing spots for his comeback. He ticked off a few of the reasons: the Spartans' history of winning football, their big and enthusiastic fan base and better facilities than he could dream of in Evanston.</p><p>"I'm just excited to have a home-field advantage," Fitzgerald said. "Never lived that. It's going to be cool."</p><p>Fitzgerald had a few chances to talk about his former team and how things ended, but he mostly focused on the Spartans. One exception was when he was asked if he had a chip on his shoulder.</p><p>"I wouldn't say I have a chip on my shoulder," Fitzgerald said. "I wouldn't say our program has a chip on our shoulder. I'd say we have a bag of chips on our shoulder. I'll leave it at that."</p><p>He was more forthcoming about his quarterback, who is familiar to Chicago-area fans. St. Francis grad Alessio Milivojevic is a redshirt sophomore who started the last four games for the 4-8 Spartans last season.</p><p>"He's just got all the leadership skills you're looking for, that 'it' factor," Fitzgerald said.</p><p>Milivojevic was a junior at St. Francis in 2022, when he met Fitzgerald — then in his final season at Northwestern — for the first time.</p><p>"Coach Fitz is a legend," Milivojevic said. "Everyone has great things to say about him. ... It's wild how worlds collide."</p><p>The fact that they're both Spartans is clear proof of that.</p>

entries.title: Democratic state lawmakers push to hold ICE accountable nationwide
entries.summary: <p>A group of Democratic state lawmakers from around the nation were in Chicago Wednesday to push for more legislation that would give the public the ability to sue U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents over fatal shootings and arrests made without warrants.</p><p>“I never imagined that I would spend the majority of my first two years in my term drafting laws and helping support laws that protect people from our own federal government,” said state Sen. Graciela Guzman, D-Chicago, who led a news conference organized by an advocacy group known as State Innovation Exchange.</p><p>“I thought we'd be talking about lowering healthcare, lowering costs, funding our schools and fighting for a more equitable Illinois. Instead, this (Donald Trump) administration has forced states like ours into a different kind of work, which is defending our communities from federal overreach.”</p><p>Last fall, Illinois became one of the few states in the country to allow residents to sue immigration agents who violate their constitutional rights to due process and protects against unreasonable searches and seizures.</p><p>House Bill 1312 was signed into law last fall. The law’s other key provision bans civil immigration arrests in and around Illinois courthouses.</p><p>Lawmakers from other states, including Georgia, Maryland, Utah, Colorado and Minnesota, said they also are pushing for protections for their residents.</p><p>“We have had federal agents break car windows and rain glass down on 1-year-old children, or throw middle-aged women to the ground who were peacefully protesting,” said Colorado state Sen. Mike Weissman. “All of us up here are state legislators who deeply believe in using the power that we have under our constitution as states to simply try to make life more livable and more dignified for our constituents.”</p><p>The shooting deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota in January and now the targeting of immigrants with expired visas at U.S. airports are examples why state lawmakers have to move fast with legislation, said Minnesota state Sen. Omar Fateh.</p><p>Fateh, whose district is on the south side of Minneapolis, said he authored legislation in early 2024 to protect Minnesotans from the violation of their rights by immigration agents. But he said his fellow lawmakers felt it was too soon, too politically risky and too hypothetical to pass.</p><p>“Beginning in late 2025, Trump sent 3,000 armed, masked, untrained agents to Minnesota. It was the largest federal invasion in American history in a state that has less than 1% of the nation's undocumented people. Trump's agents rounded up random people on the street, they arrested whole families, young children, moms and old women," Fateh said.</p><p>"They pursued, harassed, detained, arrested and jailed Minnesotans in every stage of immigration, including legal status, refugees, naturalized citizens, even second- and third-generation citizens, and then they killed two civilian observers, Renee Good and Alex Pretti,” Fateh added. “Suddenly, the fight to protect people from Trump's fascism went from being too early to seemingly too late."</p><p>Guzman, co-chair of the Illinois Latino Legislative Caucus, said five lawsuits have been filed under the new state law.</p><p><i>Michael Puente is a reporter and anchor for WBEZ. Reach him </i><a class="Link" href="mailto:mpuente@wbez.org" target="_blank" ><i><u>mpuente@wbez.org</u></i></a><i>.</i><br></p>
entries.author: Michael Puente | WBEZ

entries.title: 'Joker' producer defrauded Illinois investors in $100 million Ponzi scheme, feds say
entries.summary: <p>A Hollywood movie producer with credits on "Joker" and "Ghostbusters: Afterlife" was charged this week with running a $100 million Ponzi scheme that ensnared several Illinois investors, the Department of Justice announced.</p><p>Jason Cloth, 60, of Beverly Hills, was arrested Tuesday in Los Angeles and appeared in court there on seven counts of wire fraud, according to a statement from the U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros of the Northern District of Illinois. The indictment, filed in Illinois, was unsealed Tuesday.</p><p>Cloth operated Canada-based Creative Wealth Media Finance Corp. and, for the past seven years, solicited clients, including an investment adviser in Illinois, to invest in film and entertainment projects, prosecutors say.</p><p>Cloth got more than $100 million from the Illinois investment adviser, the adviser’s clients and other investors based on false representations, according to the indictment. Prosecutors say he actually used the money for a real estate project in Canada and other personal purposes, according to the indictment.</p><p>Cloth is accused of engaging in a Ponzi scheme by using some investor funds to repay prior investors, prosecutors say. The indictment seeks forfeiture of $12.25 million from Cloth.</p><p>Cloth is listed as the executive producer of the 2019 film "Joker," the 2022 film "Babylon" and the 2021 film "Ghostbusters: Afterlife," according to his IMDb profile.</p><p>It was not immediately clear who was representing Cloth in the case.</p><p>Cloth is a defendant in an ongoing 2024 class action lawsuit filed in Cook County alleging he owes Chicago-area investors $180 million in the same alleged Ponzi scheme. Lawyers for the plaintiffs in that case <a class="Link" href="https://www.legalnewsline.com/cook-county-record/chicago-area-investors-part-of-nationwide-180m-class-action-vs-movie-financier-jason-cloth-over/article_12e06f52-36e5-564b-9958-2e938824cc64.html" target="_blank" >say the scheme</a> allowed Cloth to get film credits and continue a "lavish lifestyle."</p><p>Lawyers in that case claim that Ponzi scheme also included investments in "Ghostbusters: Afterlife" as well as in the film "Monkey Man."</p><p>Both films were profitable, that lawsuit claims, but Cloth is accused of repaying only some investors.</p>

entries.title: Suburban cemetery workers arrested by ICE join nationwide effort to hold federal agents accountable
entries.summary: <p>Two suburban cemetery workers arrested by federal immigration agents last fall are suing the federal government as a part of nationwide American Civil Liberties Union effort attempting to hold U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement employees accountable. </p><p>The two workers, both U.S. citizens, allege they were maced and wrongly arrested by agents last October while on the job at Concordia Cemetery in Forest Park. They filed their claims in March under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows people to seek financial compensation for wrongdoing by federal government employees.</p><p>Darren Eichler and Daniel Greer were working on the cemetery grounds when they noticed immigration agents trying to arrest a man standing in the Des Plaines River, which runs alongside the cemetery. From behind the cemetery's fence, Eichler, Greer and two other co-workers told the agents to leave the area and stop harassing people, according to their complaints. </p><p>Instead, agents approached them and demanded to be let into the cemetery. When they refused, agents took out bolt cutters and cut the gate's lock, according to the complaints. The agent sprayed them with mace and arrested them. Eichler started experiencing intense chest pains and struggled to breathe. He repeatedly asked to go to the hospital, but it took agents over an hour to take him to Rush Oak Park Hospital, where he was kept handcuffed. He was eventually released from the hospital without charges, according to his complaint. </p><p>Meanwhile, Greer was sprayed, shoved to the ground and his hands were zip-tied behind his back, according to his complaint. He was taken to a Department of Homeland Security facility but was never told why he was detained or offered medical help for the chemical burns on his face. He was also released without charges, but he was handed paperwork claiming he was arrested for "assaulting or resisting an officer," according to the complaint. </p><p>“As the agents escalated their attack on us, I kept thinking that they would stop and recognize their behavior was not right,” Greer said in a statement from the ACLU. “At every step, they escalated violence and treated us like dirt.”</p><p>DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>The two men join 54 other individuals filing claims against the federal government. In the ACLU's statement, the organization said it was leading the effort to help "dozens of people and families who are seeking justice for the harm they experienced at the hands of federal immigration agents." </p>
entries.author: Kaitlin Washburn

entries.title: Acusan a tres de vandalizar y robar cámaras lectoras de placas Flock en los suburbios del oeste
entries.summary: <p>Tres hombres han sido acusados de robar y vandalizar los controversiales lectores de placas durante el fin de semana en los suburbios del oeste.</p><p>Anthony Pareigis, de 34 años; Jacob Steichmann, de 32; y Thomas Yano, de 31, enfrentan cargos por robo y daños a la propiedad gubernamental, informó la Oficina del Fiscal del Condado de DuPage.</p><p>A eso de la 1 a. m. del domingo, la policía descubrió que dos cámaras Flock habían sido vandalizadas y robadas en Lisle y que otras tres habían sido robadas de un área no incorporada del suburbio. Aproximadamente una hora después, los agentes de Lisle vieron a dos hombres vestidos de negro, con máscaras y guantes, acercarse a un lector de placas.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-5a0000" name="module-5a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Un hombre sostenía una escalera y otro, un taladro, según la oficina del fiscal. Pareigis, de Downers Grove, fue detenido, pero el otro hombre huyó.</p><p>La policía de Lisle encontró cerca un automóvil Subaru gris de 2012 con los vidrios bajados, según la oficina del fiscal, que indicó que los agentes pudieron ver cinco lectores de placas Flock en el interior, junto con una escalera plegable, unos guantes de látex negros, una sierra y herramienta eléctrica. Cada cámara Flock vale alrededor de $2,800.</p><p>Steichmann, de Downers Grove, y Yano, de Indian Head Park, fueron arrestados por la Policía de Downers Grove aproximadamente una hora más tarde.</p><p>Los tres hombres fueron acusados de dos cargos de robo a la propiedad gubernamental por montos entre $500 y $10,000 y de dos cargos de daños criminales a la propiedad. Esos no son delitos que permitan la detención, por lo que fueron liberados a la espera del juicio.</p><p>El uso de cámaras lectoras de placas se ha vuelto muy polémico. En agosto pasado, una auditoría <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/08/29/empresa-de-camaras-de-placas-de-auto-detiene-cooperacion-con-agencias-federales" target="_blank" >realizada por el secretario de Estado Alexi Giannoulias</a> reveló que Flock compartió información con la Oficina de Aduanas y Protección Fronteriza de los Estados Unidos (CBP), una de las agencias clave que llevan a cabo la política de deportaciones masivas de la administración del presidente Donald Trump.</p><p>Flock, entonces, puso en pausa los programas piloto con CBP y con las Investigaciones de Seguridad Nacional (HSI), otro brazo del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS), según Garrett Langley, fundador y director ejecutivo de la compañía.</p><p>Las comunidades de todo el país continúan cortando lazos con Flock debido a preocupaciones sobre la privacidad y la vigilancia gubernamental. Los residentes de los suburbios de Chicago han exigido lo mismo. La representante estatal Kelly Cassidy, demócrata por Chicago, presentó recientemente una legislación que busca establecer límites al uso de lectores automáticos de placas, fijando estándares sobre cuánto tiempo se pueden conservar los datos y quién puede acceder a ellos.</p><p>Otros funcionarios electos, incluido el fiscal del Condado de DuPage, Bob Berlin, han dicho que estos lectores son invaluables para la aplicación de la ley.</p><p>“Los lectores de placas no son herramientas de vigilancia de 'Big Brother'”, escribió Berlin el lunes. “Son una herramienta fundamental utilizada por las fuerzas del orden, bajo estrictas directrices legales, para localizar vehículos específicos sospechosos de estar involucrados en un delito”.</p><p>“Cualquiera que sea sorprendido dañando o robando un lector de placas enfrentará todo el peso de la ley y, de ser declarado culpable, afrontará una cantidad significativa de tiempo tras las rejas”, aseveró.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>
